summary: A 1978 note on recent extensions to the SUPDUP protocol, describing changes made since the original specification. Its status is unknown.

plainLanguage.summary: This note lists the new features added to the remote screen tool since it was first written.

subtitle: New features added to the remote terminal display protocol

tldr.problem: The SUPDUP protocol for remote terminal display was being actively developed, and new features were being added beyond the original specification.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC documents extensions including a graphics capability option, two new terminal parameters (input and output baud rates), and a new terminal option for parenthesis-bracket swapping, with notes on compatibility.
tldr.outcome: The extensions are backward compatible, so older SUPDUP implementations continue to work while newer ones can take advantage of the new features.

today: RFC 747 documents extensions to SUPDUP, a 1970s protocol for remote terminal display. The protocol and the systems that used it have been superseded by modern terminal and remote access protocols.

sections.title: SUPDUP Extensions Overview
sections.content:
RFC 747 documents recent extensions to the SUPDUP protocol, a system for displaying a remote computer's screen on a local terminal. These extensions are additions to the original SUPDUP specification, documented separately in RFC 734.

Rather than issue a completely new version of RFC 734, Mark Crispin issued this update to describe the changes. The extensions are designed to be both upward and downward compatible. Most SUPDUP user and server programs can ignore the new features and continue using the original protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: SUPDUP is a way to see a distant computer's screen on your terminal. New features were added, but old versions still work because the changes are optional.

sections.title: The New Extensions
sections.content:
Three new variables are added to the initial negotiation between the user (client) and server. The first is SMARTS, which describes the graphics capabilities of the terminal. RFC 746 documents SUPDUP's graphics extension in detail. If graphics are not being used, SMARTS is set to zero.

The second and third variables are ISPEED and OSPEED, which specify the input and output baud rates of the terminal. For example, a terminal that receives at 150 baud and sends at 1200 baud would have ISPEED of 150 and OSPEED of 1200. A speed of zero means the line speed is not known. These baud rates help the server manage buffering for the terminal.

A new bit flag has also been added to the TTYOPT field: %TPPRN, which swaps parenthesis with square brackets on input. This is useful for LISP users whose terminals have parenthesis as a shifted character but no native square brackets. This bit is normally off, and servers are not required to implement it.
sections.plainLanguage: Three new pieces of information are added: what the terminal can draw, how fast data flows in and out, and a switch for users who need parenthesis and brackets swapped.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content: These extensions are optional. Older SUPDUP implementations that do not know about the new variables will ignore them without trouble. Similarly, older terminals and implementations that do not support the new TTYOPT bit will simply have it set to zero or ignore it. Since SUPDUP is still being actively worked on, this update approach allows the protocol to evolve without requiring all implementations to update simultaneously.
sections.plainLanguage: Old versions of SUPDUP do not understand the new features, but they do not break because the new features are optional.

references.text: Stallman, R. M., "SUPDUP Graphics Extension", RFC 746, March 1978.
